content: The study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of various tests for leprosy under programmatic conditions. A systematic literature search was conducted using two electronic bibliographic databases, MEDLINE and Embase, covering publications from 1996 to January 2017. The search strategy incorporated MeSH terms and text words related to leprosy, diagnosis, sensitivity and specificity, predictive value, and diagnostic accuracy, combined using Boolean operators. No restrictions were applied regarding study design or language. The search strategy included terms for different forms of leprosy (e.g., borderline, lepromatous, multibacillary, paucibacillary, tuberculoid) and diagnostic criteria (e.g., early diagnosis, sensitivity, specificity, predictive value). Authors of major trials, researchers, and field experts were contacted to identify additional relevant literature. Reference lists of retrieved studies were reviewed, and all identified citations were exported to Reference Manager software. Eligibility criteria included cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, and case-control studies that evaluated diagnostic accuracy against a reference standard. The population included adults and children with suspected leprosy or confirmed leprosy cases, as well as non-leprosy controls. The reference standard for leprosy diagnosis was primarily based on the RJ and WHO classifications, incorporating clinical, histopathological, and bacteriological criteria. Controls included household contacts, healthy individuals, and patients with tuberculosis or other skin conditions. The diagnostic tests evaluated included ELISA tests for antibodies to PGL-1, MMP-I and II, LID, and NDO; immunochromatographic/lateral flow tests; PCR; and other tests such as M. leprae particle agglutination and skin tests using M. leprae soluble antigens. Studies reporting sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, false positives, false negatives, and direct harms were included. All potentially eligible studies were critically appraised, and any inclusion queries were discussed with a methodologist or WHO leprosy expert. Data extraction was performed using a pre-developed and piloted form. A random sample of articles was double-checked by the methodologist and WHO expert. Risk assessment focused on criteria such as case-control design, pre-specification of threshold values, and discordant data. Sensitivity and specificity data were summarized using medians and ranges. Sensitivity was calculated separately for multibacillary (MB) and paucibacillary (PB) cases, while specificity was calculated for household contacts, healthy controls, and tuberculosis patients. Likelihood ratios were calculated based on median sensitivity and specificity for healthy controls. Meta-analysis was not conducted due to heterogeneity in study designs, low study quality, and variability in cases and controls. The systematic search identified 568 citations, of which 73 full-text articles were reviewed. Ultimately, 40 studies met the inclusion criteria. The studies showed low or very low-quality evidence for all tests. ELISA tests demonstrated high sensitivity for MB cases but low sensitivity for PB cases, with generally high specificity across different control groups. PCR studies showed higher accuracy than ELISA in some cases but often relied on skin biopsy specimens and targeted different DNA fragments. No study evaluated a commercially available PCR assay. Whole blood PCR showed sensitivity of 96% for MB and 70% for PB, with specificity ranging from 93% to 100%. Other tests, such as M. leprae particle agglutination and skin tests, showed variable sensitivity and specificity, with generally low quality of evidence. Limitations of the study included the use of only two bibliographic databases, potential undiagnosed/latent leprosy among household contacts, and challenges in interpreting specificity when household contacts were used as controls. The overall evidence quality was low, and diagnostic accuracy varied significantly across tests and populations.
